tldr: A model-based reinforcement learning framework that learns directly on an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator without simulation pretraining or human demonstrations, achieving sub-centimeter mean path tracking error at high speeds with just 40 minutes of online learning.
hero_caption: Overview of the framework. A probabilistic dynamics ensemble model is updated on-the-fly using data collected on the real machine, while sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) plans path following. The exact same dynamics model handles both time-synchronized tracking and free-speed contouring.
overview:
Hydraulic construction machinery delivers immense power, but input delays, valve deadbands, strong nonlinearities, and inter-actuator coupling make fast, precise control exceptionally difficult. Machine-to-machine variations also make learning directly on hardware desirable. However, the high cost of operating heavy machinery and safety risks have historically presented steep hurdles.

To address this, the authors developed an online model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) framework that learns on hardware completely from scratch. It trains an ensemble of neural networks that models state history to capture input-output delays and accounts for uncertainty. Sampling-based MPC using MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) then generates trajectories in real time based on these predictions. Furthermore, they introduce a "precision-gated contouring objective" that conditions the progress reward on path accuracy, solving the problem of controllers recklessly cutting corners to gain speed.

In validation, the approach first demonstrated far higher sample efficiency than leading MBRL baselines (such as DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2) in a hydraulic excavator simulator. Next, it was deployed on an 11.5-ton Menzi Muck M445 excavator for pure real-world learning from scratch—without demonstrations or simulation pretraining.

Within just 20 minutes of real-world interaction, tracking accuracy matched prior learned controllers that required 100–150 minutes of data and pretraining. After 40 minutes, it achieved sub-centimeter mean path error even during high-speed operations. Peak end-effector speeds reached 180 cm/s, proving that speed does not have to come at the expense of precision.
contributions: Building an online MBRL framework that learns a probabilistic dynamics model from scratch on real hardware data to control the machine without pretraining or demonstrations.
Proposing a precision-gated contouring objective that conditions the progress reward on path accuracy, prioritizing geometric precision over speed.
Deploying on an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator to achieve sub-centimeter tracking accuracy under high-speed operation after only 40 minutes of real-world learning.

sections.heading: Why is real-time learning-based control so hard for heavy machinery?
sections.summary: Hydraulic robots have complex fluid dynamics that are notoriously difficult to model analytically. While learning directly on hardware is ideal, severe data collection costs and safety constraints on heavy equipment demand a framework that combines extreme sample efficiency with fast, highly precise control.
sections.details:
Fluid actuators, such as hydraulic and pneumatic systems, offer high power output, but they come with intricate internal dynamics. Valve deadbands (regions where inputs produce no motion), hydraulic circuit response lags, cylinder-to-cylinder coupling, and load-dependent nonlinearities make manual physics-based modeling daunting.

While data-driven approaches like deep reinforcement learning (RL) have made notable progress recently, deploying them on real hardware remains difficult. For heavy machines like hydraulic excavators, gathering data is time-consuming, expensive, and risks hardware damage. Moreover, machines of the same model often exhibit noticeable variations, highlighting the need for sample-efficient methods that can "learn directly on individual machines from brief interaction data."

The authors therefore proposed an online MBRL framework. It learns a probabilistic dynamics ensemble (a set of multiple predictors) online from real-world experience and runs sampling-based MPC (Model Predictive Control) using these predictions. To prevent the controller from taking wide turns or cutting corners in pursuit of speed, they integrated "precision-gated contouring," which only rewards progress when path error is low. The goal is to achieve fast, high-precision motion from zero prior data on an 11.5-ton excavator in a very short time.

captions.F1: The real-world online MBRL framework. The probabilistic ensemble model is updated online using real-world data, and sampling-based MPC computes control commands according to task rewards. Because the dynamics model is decoupled from the reward function, the same learned model can be reused for different objectives, such as time tracking and contouring.

sections.heading: Differences from prior work: moving beyond simulators and prioritizing precision
sections.summary: Prior heavy machinery control mostly relied on offline learning or simulators trained on real-world data. This work differs by learning directly online on hardware without intermediate simulators, and by redesigning contouring control (MPCC) trade-offs to inherently prioritize geometric precision over speed.
sections.details:
### II-A Learning-Based Control of Complex Robotic Systems
Previous control work on hydraulic and pneumatic soft robots or quadruped robots has relied heavily on model-free RL or offline system identification models. In hydraulic machinery, the dominant paradigm was a two-stage approach: learn actuator models from real data to build a simulator, train policies in simulation, and then adapt them to the real system. In contrast, this paper achieves a drastically simpler operational workflow by bypassing simulators entirely, learning dynamics directly from autonomously collected real-world data, and feeding them straight into receding-horizon planning (MPC) on the fly.

### II-B Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL)
By learning an explicit model of the environment, MBRL provides significantly higher sample efficiency than model-free alternatives. However, strong real-world non-stationarity, noise, and heavy real-time computation previously limited its deployment on large hardware. This framework achieves real-time execution on physical hardware by combining a probabilistic ensemble that captures aleatoric dynamics noise with ultrafast sampling-based MPC powered by JAX's JIT (just-in-time) compilation.

### II-C Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC)
Path following includes not just "time-based tracking" (which assigns reference setpoints at fixed timestamps) but also "contouring control (MPCC)," which progresses along a path while penalizing deviations from its geometric shape. Conventional MPCC typically sums a progress reward and a contouring error penalty. Under this additive structure, increasing the progress weight encourages the controller to cut corners and ignore tracking error. This work introduces an exact projection of sampled trajectories onto a forward reference window and a multiplicative "precision gate" that decays the progress reward as error grows, structurally prioritizing geometric accuracy over speed.

sections.heading: Capturing cascading delays and designing precision-first MPC
sections.summary: Without hydraulic pressure sensors, a probabilistic neural network models delay effects using histories of joint states and actions. Multi-step rollout training limits compounding errors, real-time MPC is handled by MPPI, and a precision gate zeros out progress rewards whenever tracking error spikes.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The control target consists of the four arm joints of a hydraulic excavator (boom, stick, telescopic arm, and bucket pitch). The control action $a_t$ represents current setpoints sent to electro-hydraulic pilot valves, and observations are joint positions $q_t$ and velocities $\dot{q}_t$. The objective is end-effector path tracking, despite valve delays, deadbands, and nonlinear actuator cross-coupling throughout the hydraulic system.

### III-B Probabilistic Dynamics Model
Because the excavator lacks hydraulic pressure sensors, hidden hydraulic states and delay dynamics must be captured indirectly. The input is therefore an extended state $s_t = [q_t, \dot{q}_t, q_{t-1}, \dot{q}_{t-1}, \dots, q_{t-k}, \dot{q}_{t-k}, a_{t-1}, \dots, a_{t-k}]$ containing histories over the past $k$ steps. Following the PETS approach, the model uses an ensemble of feedforward neural networks that outputs the Gaussian mean and variance of the next velocity, while next positions are integrated from velocities. During training, the loss evaluates not just one-step errors, but multi-step rollouts of horizon $H$ fed recursively with the model's own predictions, mitigating compounding errors.

### III-C Planning with the Learned Model
At each 40 ms control step, MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) searches for action sequences over a forward horizon of $T$ steps. For real-time tractability, MPC rollouts use the ensemble's mean prediction. In addition, an exponential moving average (EMA) filter is applied to the joint commands and evaluated within the sampling search itself, preventing jerky, high-frequency command oscillations from reaching the physical actuators.

### III-D Reward Function Design: Time Tracking and Contouring
Task definitions are fully independent of the dynamics model:
- **Time Tracking**: Penalizes errors (both joint and end-effector) relative to a time-indexed reference point.
- **Contouring**: Orthogonally projects the current position onto a forward reference window (size $K$) along the path, yielding contouring error $c$ and progress step $\Delta \phi$. Here, the authors introduce the precision-gated reward $r = \rho \Delta\phi \exp(-c^2 / \sigma^2) - c^2$. If the error $c$ exceeds the gate width $\sigma$, the progress reward decays exponentially, permitting speedups only when the path is traced accurately.

### III-E Online Learning Loop
With no initial model available, safe random sinusoidal valve currents are applied within joint limits to collect the first batch of data and train the initial ensemble. Subsequently, target joint positions are randomly sampled each episode to generate trajectories, and the robot collects data while driven by MPC. At the end of each episode, the model is retrained on all aggregated data before starting the next episode. To avoid early instability, command limits are kept small during the first few episodes and gradually expanded up to $1.0$.

sections.heading: Outperforming modern model-based RL baselines in sample efficiency
sections.summary: Using a high-fidelity excavator simulator validated in prior research, the approach was benchmarked against modern MBRL baselines (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and MBDPO). The proposed method matched 100+ episodes of baseline performance within just 20 episodes, demonstrating dramatic sample efficiency.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Setup
The evaluation used a high-fidelity hydraulic excavator simulator identified from real machine data, running 3D polynomial trajectory tracking tasks. Baseline comparisons included latent-space models DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, as well as MBDPO (which computes policy gradients through the model), all evaluated under identical data collection budgets.

### IV-B Sample Efficiency Comparison with Baselines
As shown in Figure F3, the proposed framework substantially outperformed all baselines in both model accuracy (1-step prediction MSE) and tracking error (tracking MSE).

Most striking is the learning speed early on. While the strongest baseline, MBDPO, required more than 100 episodes before showing signs of tracking, the proposed method achieved strong tracking accuracy within just 20 episodes. After 400 episodes, visible tracking deviations remained in MBDPO, whereas the proposed method traced near-perfect paths.

Why such a large difference? First, the probabilistic ensemble explicitly captures aleatoric noise (physical uncertainty), automatically down-weighting inconsistent data during training. Second, the EMA filter on control actions keeps inputs smooth, directly addressing the severe model overfitting caused by high-frequency oscillatory inputs that plagued the baselines.

captions.F3: Benchmark comparison in the simulator. Top: Model 1-step prediction MSE. Middle: Trajectory tracking MSE. Bottom: End-effector trajectories at 20, 100, and 400 episodes. The proposed method (blue) dramatically outperforms baselines like MBDPO in both convergence speed and tracking accuracy in just 20 episodes.

sections.heading: Validated on an 11.5-ton excavator: sub-centimeter accuracy in 40 minutes
sections.summary: Using an 11.5-ton Menzi Muck M445 excavator, online learning was performed completely from scratch without a simulator. Within 40 minutes of operation, mean contouring error dropped below 1 cm, and the precision gate preserved accuracy even at high end-effector speeds up to 180 cm/s.
sections.details:
### V-A Real-World Setup and Evaluation Metrics
Experiments were conducted on an 11.5-ton Menzi Muck M445 walking hydraulic excavator (Figure F4). The JAX code ran on the onboard RTX 5080 GPU and Ryzen 9 7900X CPU. MPPI computation took an average of 7.6 ms (max 8.1 ms), comfortably fitting within the 40 ms control cycle. Evaluated metrics included the contouring error $e_{\mathrm{cont}}$ (shortest distance to the path) and the velocity-normalized error $\rho_M = |e|_{\max} / v_{\max}$.

### V-B Online Learning Performance
One-hour learning runs from scratch were performed for three objectives: time tracking, pace-constrained contouring ($K=1$), and free contouring ($K=7$) (Figure F5). Across all setups, tracking error plummeted within the first 20 minutes, reaching mean contouring errors of 0.87–1.4 cm. While prior work (on an M545 excavator) required 100–150 minutes of real data and simulation pretraining, this approach reached a comparable performance level in just 20 minutes.

After 40 minutes, all modes achieved sub-centimeter mean error. Free contouring ($K=7$) ran at roughly 1.5 times the end-effector speed of time tracking (averaging over 45 cm/s) while preserving high accuracy, shortening execution time by about one-third. In high-stress tests over long-distance paths, the system achieved a peak speed of 180 cm/s (well above the 129 cm/s in prior work) while sustaining a mean error of 0.69 cm.

### V-C Balancing Speed and Accuracy: Precision Gate Ablation
To test the precision gate, standard additive MPCC (ungated) was compared against the proposed method across various progress weights $\rho$ (Figure F6). In the ungated version, raising $\rho$ to increase speed caused aggressive corner-cutting and degraded geometric accuracy. In contrast, the precision-gated controller kept errors tightly bounded even as speeds rose, closely adhering to the reference geometry. Mathematical analysis confirms that while the break-even error grows as $\sqrt{\rho}$ without the gate, it grows far more slowly as $\sqrt{W(\rho)} \approx \sqrt{\log \rho}$ with the gate (where $W$ is the Lambert W function).

### V-D Task Independence
To test whether the dynamics models overfitted to specific tasks, a $3 \times 3$ cross-evaluation was conducted combining models frozen at 60 minutes with the three reward objectives. All combinations performed well simply by switching the objective, confirming that the learned dynamics transfer directly across different tasks.

captions.F5: Online learning progress from scratch on hardware. Top: (a) Contouring error, (b) joint error, (c) end-effector speed, and (d) trajectory duration. Bottom: Snapshots of end-effector paths for the $K=7$ mode at 3, 10, 20, and 60 minutes. Clean tracking emerges in just 20 minutes.

(c),(d) Trajectory comparison at weight $\rho=160$. The ungated version (c) cuts corners, whereas the gated version (d) travels fast while preserving geometric fidelity.

sections.heading: A new bar for real-world learning: future directions and challenges
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that online MBRL without prior knowledge is practical on complex hydraulic heavy machinery. Next steps include moving from free-space motions to contact-rich tasks like earthmoving, using uncertainty for safe exploration, and integrating external perception.
sections.details:
This paper shows that on an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator—a massive, highly nonlinear system—high-precision, high-speed control can be acquired online within tens of minutes on hardware without prior knowledge or simulators. In particular, the precision-gated contouring formulation offers a versatile concept for other robotics domains facing speed-accuracy trade-offs, such as autonomous driving and drone racing.

The authors outline several key avenues for future work:
- **Extending to Contact-Rich Tasks**: The current experiments focused on free-space motions; actual excavation introduces varying payloads and bucket-soil interaction forces, requiring the integration of force feedback.
- **Uncertainty-Aware Active Exploration and Safety**: The variance across the ensemble could be used to guide exploration into unvisited states or incorporated into risk-aware planning to preempt unsafe maneuvers.
- **Integration with Environment Perception**: Operating on real, unstructured construction sites will require incorporating exteroceptive sensors like cameras and LiDAR for obstacle detection and collision-avoidance planning.

takeaways: Even without dedicated hydraulic pressure sensors, incorporating past joint input-output histories into the state adequately models actuation delays.
Applying an error-dependent exponential decay gate to progress rewards theoretically and experimentally eliminates the corner-cutting problem inherent in conventional MPCC.
Training on multi-step forward rollouts rather than single-step errors, paired with action smoothing filters, is critical for stabilizing real-world MBRL.
limitations: Validation is limited to non-contact free-space trajectory tracking, leaving excavation loads and payload variations unaddressed.
Prediction uncertainty from the ensemble is not yet actively utilized for exploration guidance or safety-limit monitoring (risk avoidance).
The system lacks exteroceptive obstacle detection and collision avoidance, assuming an open workspace free of external hazards.
